title: The Georgian Terrace Hotel
description:
The Georgian Terrace Hotel, inaugurated in 1911, has long been a favored venue for an array of social gatherings, including tea dances, luncheons, and concerts—highlighted by prestigious events such as the premiere of 'Gone with the Wind.' Rising ten stories tall, its exterior featured pristine white brick complemented by opulent marble floors, majestic columns, and embellished with gold framing accents in the enduring Renaissance style.

Originally, the hotel boasted a striking tile-buttressed shed roof cornice, elegantly supported by ornate paired brackets; however, this distinctive architectural element was regrettably removed in 1945.

Conceived as a masterpiece of design, the original 10-story Georgian Terrace Hotel was meticulously planned to align with Atlanta's early trolley rail lines, converging at the intersection of Peachtree Street and Ponce de Leon Avenue. It held the distinction of being among the earliest hotels constructed beyond the bustling downtown business district, nestled within a once-quaint residential neighborhood.

title: W. W. Orr  Doctor's Building
description:
The W. W. Orr Doctors' Building, an Art Deco skyscraper constructed in 1930, stands in the southern part of Midtown Atlanta, near Peachtree Street, a prominent thoroughfare. Nearby attractions include the Georgia Aquarium, World of Coca-Cola, Centennial Olympic Park, CNN Center, Georgia Dome, Philips Arena, and the Fox Theatre. It's easily accessible via Interstate 75/85 Downtown Connector and MARTA, Atlanta's public transit.

The 11-story Orr Doctors' Building replaced a converted apartment building destroyed by fire, specifically designed for medical professionals and built to be fireproof. Renowned architectural firm Pringle & Smith, known for their Beaux Arts work, adapted to the Art Deco style for this building. The structure employed reinforced concrete and a steel service core, pioneering high-rise construction of its time.

The subtle Art Deco ornamentation emphasizes its scientific and engineering nature. Notably, the Orr Building marked a shift away from downtown Atlanta, driven by modern amenities and automobile accessibility, influencing the northward expansion of Peachtree Street.

Remarkably, the Orr Building has continuously served its intended purpose and remains under the ownership of Emory Crawford Long Hospital. Designated as a Landmark Building by the City of Atlanta in 1989, its historical and functional preservation reflects its enduring legacy.

title: Medical Arts Building
description:
The Medical Arts Building, an elegant early American skyscraper, opened its doors on February 16, 1927. It was conceived by the renowned architect G. Lloyd Preacher, a prominent figure in the early 20th-century South whose designs and architectural contributions reshaped Atlanta's cityscape. This remarkable structure was the brainchild of four distinguished local doctors - Cliff Sauls, Grady E. Clay, James E. Paulin, and Malvern D. Huff. Their vision responded to the increasing demand for cutting-edge medical offices and retail spaces in the area. The success of this venture inspired the creation of a similar establishment, the W.W. Orr Building, just north at 478 Peachtree Street, a mere three years later.

Adorned with tan brick and a limestone base, the building was graced with Beaux-Arts decorative elements like limestone pilasters, representing a significant advancement in the medical field. It not only offered state-of-the-art medical equipment but also a range of notable amenities. It featured one of Atlanta's earliest covered parking garages, reflecting the growing influence of automobiles on architectural design. Inside the building, one could discover a cafeteria, telegraph office, drugstore, and the Junior League Tearoom, which formally opened during a special preview event on February 15, 1927, staffed by Junior League volunteers. The building even housed its own post office. With a sprawling 89,000 square feet dedicated to healthcare, the Medical Arts Center was equipped with the finest medical technology and hosted special medical events, including children's clinics, further enhancing its significance.

title: Metropolitan Building
description:
The Metropolitan Theatre and Office Building was completed in 1920 at a cost of $500,000. Designed with the possibility of future expansion through additional stories, it featured a Gothic architectural style, constructed primarily using steel and brick. The building stood six stories tall, including a sizable basement. The ground floor housed a motion picture theatre with a seating capacity of 2,250, while the lower floor accommodated 1,100 seats. Additionally, there was a spacious balcony and gallery.

One of the building's most notable features was its safety arrangements, as it was entirely constructed from fireproof materials. Multiple exits along the ground floor allowed for the rapid evacuation of the theatre directly onto the street. The theater's design was the work of C.H. Howell, a specialist in amusement house construction from New York, renowned among the country's famous architects.

Situated on a lot measuring 50x182 feet, the building occupied a prime location facing Broad, Luckie, and Forsyth streets, opposite The Piedmont Hotel. This property was owned by the estate of the late J.R. Gray, the former editor of the Atlanta Journal.

On Monday, July 4, the Metropolitan Theatre opened its doors to the public at noon. The establishment was the property of Sig Samuels.

title: The Palmer Apartments
description:
In either late 1906 or early 1907, the S. H. Phelan Co. commissioned the architectural firm Norrman and Faulkner to create plans for an apartment building in the rear section of the Phelan property located at 790 Peachtree Street. The official building permit, issued on June 28, 1907, was granted to the firm of Donaldson (Reuben D.) and Pearson. According to the details provided in the building permit, the structure was designed to encompass five stories, constructed with reinforced brick walls and featuring a tile roof. The thickness of the walls ranged from 21 inches on the ground floor to 12 inches on the fifth floor. The estimated cost for this project was set at $70,000.00. The construction of the Palmer Apartments was successfully completed on March 18, 1908, with the building's ground dimensions measuring 60 feet by 78 feet.

title: The Crescent Apartments
description:
The Crescent Apartments, also recognized as the "Margaret Mitchell House," came into existence in 1899 under the ownership of Cornelius Sheehan, a member of one of Atlanta's earliest Catholic families. Originally conceived as a single-family residence, the architectural design was attributed to a previously unheralded local architect, known solely by the surname Dunning. This historic dwelling stands as one of the precious few residential vestiges that have withstood the commercialization and reconstruction of the entire Peachtree corridor, stretching from Downtown to the city limits at Brookhaven.

In 1906, Cornelius Sheehan transferred ownership of this stately residence. Today, the house holds a distinguished place on the National Register of Historic Places, commemorated for its connection to Margaret Mitchell (1900-1949). Mitchell and her husband John Marsh made Apartment #1 their home from July 1925 until the autumn of 1932. Affectionately referred to by Mitchell and her friends as "The Dump," this abode bears witness to a fascinating chapter in literary history.
